Complete Empirical Research Plan

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Chosen method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) augmented with an event-time leads/lags event-study graph.  

Justification  
• The institutional setting offers clearly dated, economy-wide regulatory shocks that exogenously alter the degree of information asymmetry (e.g., SEC Regulation Fair Disclosure, October 23 2000).  
• We can cleanly separate “high-asymmetry” firms (small-cap, thinly traded, high PIN) from “low-asymmetry” firms that should be only minimally affected.  
• DID compares changes in return-generating processes for treated vs. control stocks before and after the shock, delivering causal estimates of how information-asymmetry‐based asset-pricing models perform relative to standard models.  
• The high-frequency panel (daily data, 1990-2010) with many firms satisfies the requirements for DID with firm and time fixed effects.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for firms ex-ante in the top quartile of a pre-event information-asymmetry proxy (PIN, bid-ask spread, or the inverse of analyst coverage) measured over 1999Q1-2000Q2. Treated firms are presumed to have the greatest reduction in private information after Reg FD.  

Control group  
Firms in the bottom quartile of the same proxy (low information asymmetry). These firms form the counterfactual trend in returns and pricing-error dynamics.  

Treatment timing / event date  
Event date: October 23 2000 (announcement + enforcement of Reg FD).  
Define Post = 1 for observations with trading day ≥ Oct 24 2000, 0 otherwise. We will also explore ±12-month symmetric windows and an extended ±36-month window.  

No running variable & cutoff are required because we do not use RDD.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of Reg FD, high- and low-asymmetry firms would have followed parallel paths in pricing errors and abnormal returns.  
 Plausibility: Pre-1999–2000 lead-lag plots can be inspected; previous literature shows parallel trends across small vs. large firms over short horizons when controls are included.  

A2. No contemporaneous shocks differentially affecting the two groups around the event.  
 Plausibility: The dot-com crash overlaps the event but affects tech and non-tech firms alike; we will include industry×time fixed effects and re-run analyses excluding tech firms.  

A3. Stable group classification: Firms’ treatment status (quartile) must not change endogenously because of the reform.  
 Plausibility: Treatment is defined using only pre-period data, so Reg FD cannot influence classification.  

A4. No spillovers: Reg FD’s disclosure rules should not increase asymmetry for low-PIN firms.  
 Plausibility: Regulation is intended to reduce information gaps; any spillovers bias against finding effects.  

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Non-parallel pre-trends  
 • Mitigation: Plot event-time coefficients (-8 to ‑1 quarters). If significant, narrow the window or match on propensity scores until pre-trends disappear.  

T2. Simultaneous macro events (dot-com bust, decimalization)  
 • Mitigation: (i) include time×industry fixed effects; (ii) run placebo DID on earlier/ later placebo dates; (iii) exclude Nasdaq tech firms and replicate.  

T3. Selection bias from delistings / survival  
 • Mitigation: Use CRSP delisting returns; re-weight observations with inverse probability of survival; check robustness on balanced panel.  

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed-effects
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data Loading -----------------------------------------------------------
prices   <- fread("daily_prices.csv")       # date, permno, ret, prc
volumes  <- fread("daily_volume.csv")       # date, permno, volume
chars    <- fread("firm_chars.csv")         # permno, date, mktcap, bm
pin      <- fread("pin_proxy.csv")          # permno, yearqtr, pin

# 2. Variable Construction --------------------------------------------------
# Merge daily data
dt <- merge(prices, volumes, by = c("permno","date"))
dt <- merge(dt, chars,  by = c("permno","date"), all.x = TRUE)

# Excess return (assuming rf file):
rf <- fread("riskfree_daily.csv")  # date, rf
dt <- merge(dt, rf, by = "date")
dt[, exret := ret - rf]

# Attach PIN quartile based on 1999Q1–2000Q2 average -----------------------
pin_base <- pin[yearqtr %between% c("1999Q1","2000Q2"),
                .(pin_base = mean(pin, na.rm=TRUE)), by = permno]

# Quartile cutoffs
cut <- quantile(pin_base$pin_base, probs = c(0.25,0.75), na.rm=TRUE)
pin_base[, treated := (pin_base > cut[2])]        # 1 = top quartile
pin_base[, control := (pin_base < cut[1])]

# Keep only treated & control stocks
dt <- merge(dt, pin_base[,.(permno,treated)], by="permno")
dt <- dt[treated==TRUE | treated==FALSE]

# Event time variables ------------------------------------------------------
event_date <- as.Date("2000-10-23")
dt[, post := date >= event_date]
dt[, time_fe := format(date, "%Y-%m")]            # monthly FE
dt[, permno := as.factor(permno)]                 # firm FE

# 3. Main DID Regression ----------------------------------------------------
reg_main <- feols(exret ~ post*treated + bm + log(mktcap) |
                  permno + time_fe,
                  data = dt, cluster = ~permno)

summary(reg_main)

# 4. Event-study Leads & Lags ----------------------------------------------
dt[, rel_qtr := as.integer(floor(as.numeric(difftime(date, event_date, units="days"))/90))]
for(k in -8:8) dt[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(rel_qtr==k)*treated]

leadlag_fml <- paste("exret ~", paste(paste0("D", -8:8), collapse="+"), 
                     "+ bm + log(mktcap) | permno + time_fe")
reg_leadlag <- feols(as.formula(leadlag_fml), data = dt, cluster = ~permno)

iplot(reg_leadlag, xlab="Quarters from Reg FD", ref.line = -0.5)

# 5. Robustness: Propensity-Score Matched Sample ----------------------------
# quick PSM using logit on 1999 characteristics
library(MatchIt)
ps_data <- unique(dt[year(date)==1999,
                     .(permno, treated, mktcap, bm, avg_ret = mean(exret,na.rm=TRUE))])

m.out <- matchit(treated ~ log(mktcap) + bm + avg_ret,
                 data = ps_data, method="nearest", ratio=1)

matched_permnos <- data.table(permno = ps_data$permno[rownames(m.out$match.matrix)])
dt_match <- dt[permno %in% matched_permnos$permno]

reg_match <- feols(exret ~ post*treated + bm + log(mktcap) |
                   permno + time_fe, data = dt_match, cluster = ~permno)
summary(reg_match)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Theory (Easley & O’Hara 2004) predicts that reducing information asymmetry lowers expected returns that compensate uninformed investors, especially for high-PIN stocks.  
Hence, coefficient β₁ (post × treated) is expected to be negative: abnormal returns of high-asymmetry stocks fall by ≈ 20–40 bps per month (≈ 2.5–5 % annually) relative to controls. The magnitude roughly matches historical “information premium” estimates.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually and statistically verified ............ 0.8  
C2: No interference / spillovers across units .................................... 0.7  
C3: No simultaneous shocks differentially correlated with treatment ............... 0.6  
C4: Stable unit treatment value / consistency .................................... 0.9  
C5: Correct functional form / no compositional bias ............................... 0.8  

(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = doubtful. Values are subjective probabilities.)

Overall, with careful robustness checks, the design should yield credible causal evidence on how asymmetric-information asset-pricing models explain returns and on the efficiency implications of large information-environment shocks.
